newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Germany to do all to meet Maastricht-Waigel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany to do all to meet Maastricht-Waigel.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel predicted on Monday that unemployment would show only a slight rise in February and said his country would do everything it can to fulfil criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We will do everything to meet these criteria, including the deficit goal," Waigel told reporters before a conference with Nordic and Baltic finance ministers.
He said the latest German unemployment figures -- a record 4.66 million in January -- fitted into the country's plans to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria.

Asked if he expected joblessness to rise to 4.8 million, as reported in the Bild newspaper on Sunday, Waigel later said: "I believe the number will rise only slightly in February, not the figure that was reported. It will be roughly the same as January, perhaps a bit more.
"Then, I believe that in March and the months after that it will fall again," Waigel told Reuters.
German February unemployment data are due to be released on Thursday.

The surge to 4.66 million jobless in January, the highest level since the 1930s depression, raised concern about Germany's sputtering economic recovery and its ability to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
Waigel earlier repeated government predictions that unemployment in 1997 would average about 4.1 million, up from 3.9 million last year.
High unemployment hurts the cash-strapped government's efforts to cut its deficit by reducing tax revenues while boosting outlays for unemployment benefits.
The single currency, or euro, is scheduled to be launched on January 1, 1999. But 1997 economic data will be used to decide which EU members take part at the start.
The Maastricht Treaty sets a budget deficit ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year for candidate countries to qualify for the launch of the single currency.
The German government has projected a budget deficit target of 2.9 percent of GDP, but analysts question whether it can achieve it.

"We have included the new unemployment figures, which are worse than we had expected half a year ago, in the 2.9 percent (target). But of course we now have to wait to see how the figures are, not just in February, but in the next few months.
"We expect in the spring, early summer a positive trend will be noticed in the labour market and that the figures will fall," he said.
Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink, who was also in Bergen for the Baltic Sea conference, said: "It is hard to see monetary union taking place without the participation of Germany".
But he expected Bonn to meet the criteria.
"The German political willingness to do this is very strong," Asbrink told Reuters.

In Bonn, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Sunday attacked what he called "irresponsible" market speculation that Germany was seeking a delay of EMU and strongly reaffirmed that Bonn wanted the project to start as scheduled.
